doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: The musicians' union and shrinking orchestras
summary: Shear says the union handles synthesizers poorly and pit orchestras have dwindled since the 60s; audiences don't notice.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Do you have to join another union?
No, no. As long as you belong to the American Federation [of Musicians]. Yeah.
Okay. How is the union — I don’t want to get too sidetracked here, because this stuff is fascinating to me — but —
The union — how is it handling this business about the synthesizers and the studios —

They don’t represent the musicians at all. It’s a musicians’ union but they keep on making deals — they keep on making deals with people who they need to make deals with, and the musicians are the last to get what’s ever fair. So they don’t handle it well. The pits in the orchestras and for shows are being — constantly being cut. The fees — the money isn’t going down but the quantity of musicians are fewer. And so instead of back in the 80s when I was doing some shows in the theater district in Los Angeles, we had 15 strings, now we’ve got two keyboards and maybe four strings. And then we have two woodwind players playing 15 woodwind instruments. And it’s one or two trumpets instead of four. A lot has happened. And it didn’t start in the 80s, it started in the 60s, you know, as the years went on the number of musicians would dwindle. And the union really doesn’t stand up for you very much.
Don’t you wish that the audience would stand up and say, “I want an orchestra”?
It sounds big, they turn up the bass and they turn up the keyboard, and it sounds big. And the audience is fulfilled.

It is stunning. Because we have Broadway Theater tickets, or we did, in Utica. And I had second row seats and I could always look down, “oh my God there’s like six people down there.” And the technology —
It’s just so perfect that you almost say to yourself well you might as well just have nobody. I don’t mean that but —

Well it’s going there because the synthesizers can duplicate strings beautifully. So they don’t need strings. They might need a couple of horns here and there, trumpet, trombone, French horn, woodwinds. Because the synthesizers aren’t really perfectly duplicating the breath that you need to play an instrument like that. So it would sound a little squirrely. But strings sound beautiful on synthesizers and there’s hardly anybody down there anymore.
